1.title: The Storm Over Whitby
1.description: Half of Whitby has climbed the East Cliff to watch the sea go white. By evening a bank of fog stands off the harbour like a wall, and out of it comes a schooner under full sail, running straight at the pier with no hand at her wheel that anyone can see. The coastguard's searchlight finds her name, Demeter, as she drives up onto the sand below the churchyard. Something large and grey leaps from her deck and is gone up the Abbey steps before anyone can shout. Lucy has taken hold of your sleeve. You have had no letter from Jonathan for weeks, and you have stopped saying so.

options.label: Take Lucy home before the fog reaches the crescent.
options.detail: She has slept badly all week, and the sea tonight is no place for her.

quote.speaker: Lucy
quote.text: Mina, you are shaking, and I do not think it is the cold.

options.outcome: Mrs Westenra's fire is lit and the shutters are closed against the weather. Through the plaster you hear the coastguard's signal guns until midnight. By morning the whole town has a story, and you have only heard it second-hand.

options.label: Go down to the pier with the coastguard and the crowd.
options.detail: A wreck with a dead man at the wheel is news, and you have your shorthand notebook.

quote.speaker: Coastguard
quote.text: Stand back, miss. There is a man at that wheel and he is past waving.

options.outcome: They cut him down in the searchlight. His hands are bound to the spokes and a crucifix is wound through the knots, as if he had tied it there himself. Whitby takes its caps off. You write it all down steadily and are sick afterwards behind a stack of fish boxes.

options.label: Slip past the cordon and copy the ship's log.
options.detail: A captain's last words may name the cargo, and the Board of Trade will seal the book by morning.

quote.speaker: Young officer
quote.text: If it is shorthand, miss, I suppose it is not evidence. Be quick about it.

success.outcome: A young coastguard officer, flattered and half asleep, lets you copy the last pages. The cargo was fifty boxes of earth, consigned to a London solicitor. The crew went over the side one by one. The mate wrote, near the end, that something walked the ship at night.

failure.outcome: The officer remembers himself halfway down the third page and hands you back to Lucy with a lecture. You have a fragment of the log and a feeling of having been watched from the Abbey steps.

2.title: The Seat on the East Cliff
2.description: Old Mr Swales is dead. They found him this morning on the bench that the town says stands over a suicide's grave, his neck broken and his face turned to the sea. A week ago he told you that the dead in the churchyard come up for anyone who sits too long among them. Tonight you wake at two to find Lucy's bed empty and her slippers beside it. The street door stands open. Mrs Westenra is asleep and will not wake easily.

options.label: Go out after her alone, and at once.
options.detail: Every minute she is out of doors in a nightdress is a minute for something to happen.

quote.speaker: Mina
quote.text: I did not stop to put on a hat. I could see the seat from the top of the road.

success.outcome: You find her on the seat, asleep, with a long dark shape bending over her. You cry out and run. It lifts its head, you see two points of red, and then the cloud covers the moon. When you reach the seat she is alone, cold and breathing, with two small marks at her throat. You pin your shawl across them and walk her home.

failure.outcome: You search the cliff path in the dark and find her too late, on her back on the seat, cold to the touch. The marks are there, at her throat. You get her home. In the morning she cannot say where she has been.

options.label: Wake the household and go out with the gardener and two maids.
options.detail: Slower, but you will not be alone if you find something.

quote.speaker: Mrs Westenra
quote.text: Lucy walks in her sleep? She has not done it since she was a child. It must be the sea air.

options.outcome: By the time the lanterns reach the seat, Lucy is sitting up, confused and chilled, and nothing else is there. The maids tell the cook by breakfast. By noon half the crescent knows that Miss Lucy walks in her sleep, and Mrs Westenra will not forgive you for the talk.

options.label: Go to the seat, but send the watchman's boy after you with a lantern.
options.detail: Quicker, and a second pair of eyes may see what yours do not.

quote.speaker: Watchman's boy
quote.text: She is not hurt, miss? She is very white. I will fetch Mrs Westenra.

options.outcome: You reach the seat as the boy's lantern comes up behind you. Lucy is sitting upright with her eyes closed, her nightdress wet with dew. At her throat are two small marks, close together. You think of the pin in your shawl and tell yourself that is what it was. The boy says nothing, which is kind of him.

echoes.text: You know what stood on the steps. You have told no one, and you are keeping it as carefully as you keep your accounts.
The log in your notebook says fifty boxes of earth. Whitby has not asked what earth is for.
You have seen a dead man tied to a ship's wheel, and you have not mentioned it at breakfast.
You have half a page of the Demeter's log and a good memory for the rest.
You called out to a man on the steps and he turned round. You have not got over it.

3.title: A Letter from Buda-Pesth
3.description: Mr Hawkins forwards a letter that comes by the morning post. It is from a Sister Agatha of the Hospital of St Joseph and St Mary in Buda-Pesth, and it is written in careful English. Jonathan Harker has been in her care for some weeks. He arrived with a brain fever and cannot be questioned. He has asked for you by name, and for the Sister to say that he is well enough to marry, if you will still have him. He raves, she writes, of wolves and blood and of things she will not put on paper. Lucy is pale again this morning and says it is the heat.

options.label: Go to Buda-Pesth at once.
options.detail: Mr Hawkins will pay the fare. Lucy will have her mother and the doctor.

quote.speaker: Lucy
quote.text: Go, Mina. I shall be perfectly well. I shall write every day and tell you nothing at all.

options.outcome: You pack in an hour. Lucy kisses you at the station and tells you she is perfectly well, and you believe her only because you wish to. The train takes you away from the sea.

options.label: Stay with Lucy and send Mr Hawkins's clerk to bring Jonathan home.
options.detail: Lucy is ill and you cannot leave her. A steady clerk can fetch a sick man as well as you can.

quote.speaker: Mr Hawkins
quote.text: Harker will be brought to you, my dear. The clerk is a careful man, and I shall pay for all of it.

options.outcome: You write to the Sister, and to the hospital chaplain, and to Mr Hawkins. For ten days you nurse Lucy through two more bad nights. When the clerk telegraphs, he says only that Mr Harker is fit to travel and not fit to talk.

options.label: Go, but write first to Dr Seward and Arthur Holmwood.
options.detail: Both love Lucy and both will look in on her, if you ask.

quote.speaker: Dr Seward
quote.text: Miss Westenra will not lack a physician. Tell Mr Harker that I am glad of him.

options.outcome: Two letters go out before you do. Arthur answers by telegraph within the hour and Seward by return of post, and both say what you hoped: that Lucy will not be left alone. It is a comfort that lasts as far as Hull.

echoes.text: The two marks on Lucy's throat have not healed. She says they itch.
Mrs Westenra has told two neighbours that Lucy walks in her sleep, and the neighbours have told others.

4.title: The Hospital of St Joseph and St Mary
4.description: Jonathan is sitting up in a white room that smells of lime and iron. His hair has gone white. He is thin, and he flinches from doors, and when you say his name he weeps. He gives you a small book tied with a ribbon and sealed with wax, and asks you not to open it unless some solemn duty requires it. He says he does not want to know it again. Sister Agatha stands at the window and says the chaplain could marry you this afternoon.

options.label: Marry him this afternoon, with the journal unopened.
options.detail: He asked you not to read it. You can keep a promise.

quote.speaker: Jonathan
quote.text: Keep it, and do not read it. If I am wrong about what is in it, I should like to stay wrong.

options.outcome: The chaplain is a tired, kind man. Sister Agatha is your witness and cries into her sleeve. You are Mrs Harker by four o'clock. The little book goes into your bag with the wax unbroken, under your gloves.

options.label: Read the journal tonight while he sleeps.
options.detail: Whatever it is, it is what broke him. You would rather know it than guess.

quote.speaker: Jonathan's journal
quote.text: I write this in shorthand because I will not have it read by anyone who has not been where I have been.

options.outcome: You read it in the white room by a night lamp with Jonathan breathing beside you. When you reach the three women you put the book down and go to the window. In the morning you marry him anyway. You say nothing about the book, and he does not ask.

options.label: Sit with the Sister and ask what he said in his fever.
options.detail: She was in the room when he raved. She has not told the doctors everything.

quote.speaker: Sister Agatha
quote.text: He spoke of a count, and of wolves that came when he called. I did not know whether to pray or to send for the doctor.

options.outcome: She tells you what she heard: a count, a castle, a long line of boxes, and a name that he said over and over, which she took to be a place. You marry him the next morning. The name is the only thing in your head all through the service.

5.title: Hillingham in September
5.description: By the first week of September Lucy cannot get out of bed. She has lost her colour and her appetite, and she breathes as if she were climbing stairs. Dr Seward, who loved her and was refused, has sent to Amsterdam for his old teacher, Professor Van Helsing. The Professor arrives in a hansom with two bags and a case of surgical instruments. He looks at Lucy for a long time. Then he asks for a basin, a box of garlic flowers from Haarlem, and the names of everyone who has been in the room. Mrs Westenra says the room now smells like a drain.

options.label: Offer your arm for the transfusion.
options.detail: Four men have given blood already. The Professor says she needs another, and he will not take a man who is shaking.

quote.speaker: Van Helsing
quote.text: You are brave, Madam Mina, and I am sorry for it. Sit here and look at the ceiling.

options.outcome: You lie on the sofa with your sleeve rolled and look at the ceiling rose. It takes forty minutes. Lucy's colour comes back a little, and yours goes. Jonathan sits at your head and does not speak.

options.label: Keep the room as the Professor asks: garlic at the window and flowers round her neck.
options.detail: It makes no medical sense, and Dr Seward does it without argument.

quote.speaker: Mrs Westenra
quote.text: Garlic, Mina! The whole house smells of it. Lucy says the flowers are ugly.

options.outcome: You hang the flowers and rub the sashes. The smell is fierce. Lucy sleeps better than she has in weeks, and the maids give notice by Thursday.

options.label: Make Mrs Westenra understand why the window must stay shut.
options.detail: She is frightened for Lucy and wants air for her. She also does not like the Professor.

quote.speaker: Mrs Westenra
quote.text: A sick girl wants air, my dear. I have nursed three husbands' worth of fevers and I know what I know.

success.outcome: It takes an hour, a cup of tea and a great deal of patience. At the end of it she pats your hand and agrees to leave the flowers where they are. That night Lucy sleeps through, and the Professor says so at breakfast, and says nothing else.

failure.outcome: You are overruled with great kindness. In the night Mrs Westenra opens the window and takes the flowers away, to give her daughter some peace. In the morning Lucy is found bled white, and the Professor's face when he sees her is something you will remember.

echoes.text: The Professor asks about the marks on Lucy's throat. You are the only one who can say when you first saw them.
You have read what happened at the castle. You do not say so to the Professor yet. You watch his face when he says the word 'vampire'.
You left Lucy at Whitby, and she was worse when you came back.
Dr Seward and Arthur both called at Hillingham while you were away, which is why the Professor was sent for before you were back.
You were with her through all of August and saw each of the bad nights.
Jonathan's ravings come back to you at odd hours: a count, a castle, a long row of boxes.

6.title: The Night the Window Broke
6.description: On the night of the twentieth the glass comes in. A grey wolf, loose from the Zoological Gardens, puts its head and shoulders through Lucy's window and lies there growling among the flowers. Mrs Westenra, who has been sitting up with her daughter, dies in her chair before anyone reaches her. The maids are found asleep in the kitchen and cannot be woken for hours. By morning Lucy is lying very still, and the Professor, kneeling beside her, says that he does not think she will see the evening.

options.label: Stay with Lucy until the end, and hold her hand.
options.detail: Her mother is dead, and the Professor will not leave the other room. Somebody should be here who loves her.

quote.speaker: Lucy
quote.text: Mina, I am so tired. Will you see that Arthur is told, gently, by someone he likes?

options.outcome: She is awake near the end and quite clear. She asks you to write to Arthur and tell him she was not afraid. A little before sunset she sleeps, and her face looks younger than you have seen it since Exeter. You do not notice, until later, that her teeth look different.

options.label: Take charge of the house: the dead woman, the maids, the police and the solicitor.
options.detail: Someone has to, and the men are no use here.

quote.speaker: Jonathan
quote.text: I never saw anyone do what you did today. I could not have thought of half of it.

options.outcome: By midday the doctor has signed one certificate, the police have taken the wolf away in a van, and the maids are in the scullery with brandy. You are tired in a way that has nothing to do with sleep. Lucy dies at four, with the Professor and Dr Seward at her side, and you are not there.

options.label: Go to the station with Dr Seward's telegram and meet Arthur's train yourself.
options.detail: He loves her. He should hear it from a friend and not from a porter.

quote.speaker: Arthur
quote.text: I was too late, wasn't I? Please do not tell me that I was not. I would rather know the truth.

options.outcome: Arthur's train is forty minutes late and he is grey when he steps down. He asks you for the truth and you give it to him, standing on the platform with the steam going up round you. He holds your arm all the way to Hillingham. He thanks you, in the hall, for not lying.

echoes.text: You are Mrs Harker now. The maids at Hillingham call you that, and you have not yet got used to it.
The window was shut and the garlic was on the sill. The wolf came through them anyway.
Mrs Westenra opened the window against advice two nights ago. You have not said so aloud.
The flowers are still round Lucy's neck. The Professor will not let anyone take them away.

7.title: Dr Seward's Study
7.description: Seven weeks after the storm, at the asylum at Purfleet, you spread the papers on Dr Seward's desk: Jonathan's journal in your typing, Seward's phonograph cylinders transcribed, your own diary, Lucy's letters, the Demeter's log, the cuttings. Professor Van Helsing reads all night. In the morning he stands up and says what has been waiting in the room since the storm. A man named Count Dracula, who is not what he seems, has bought the house next door and brought fifty boxes of his native earth to England. He means to stay. There are five men and one woman in the study. The Professor asks for a plan.

options.label: Follow the Professor's way: find the boxes and make them unfit for him with the Host and the rite.
options.detail: The boxes are his ground. Take away the ground, and he has nowhere to lie by day.

quote.speaker: Van Helsing
quote.text: Each box we sanctify is a door we close. He has fifty doors. We have a little bread, and a great deal of patience.

options.outcome: The room agrees, Quincey Morris with a drawl and Arthur with a nod. Jonathan watches you rather than the Professor. You say that you will keep the record of every box that is closed, and Van Helsing says that is the most useful thing that anyone has offered yet.

options.label: Follow the paper: trace the boxes through the solicitor, the carters and the railway.
options.detail: Fifty boxes do not move themselves. Somebody drove a cart, and somebody signed for them.

quote.speaker: Jonathan
quote.text: Billington and Son took the delivery at Whitby. Carter, Paterson and Company carted it to Purfleet. A man who leaves a trail of receipts can be found.

options.outcome: Jonathan takes up the idea as if it were a drink of water. By noon he has a list of names, and you have sorted it into a table, and Quincey has pinned a pin into London for each delivery that came up from Whitby. The Professor says nothing for a minute. Then he says that he is a very old man, and he has never been so pleased to be shown a timetable.

options.label: Tell them about the dreams, and ask the Professor to put you under.
options.detail: Since Whitby you have dreamed of the sea at night, and of a voice. If the Count can see you, you may be able to see him.

quote.speaker: Van Helsing
quote.text: Madam Mina, you are offering me a window into the enemy's house. I do not like it. I am going to accept.

options.outcome: Jonathan stands up, then sits down again. Dr Seward says that it is unwise. Arthur says that he would rather it were him. The Professor says that it cannot be done with anyone else, and that if Mrs Harker is certain, he will not forbid her. You say that you are certain. You are not, but you are the only person in the room who has been looked at by him.

options.label: Ask first to see the patient in the next room: Renfield.
options.detail: He eats flies and spiders and says that the Master is coming. Seward thinks he knows more than he says.

quote.speaker: Dr Seward
quote.text: He has been very quiet since Lucy died. I have a feeling that he is waiting. I should like you to see him, Mrs Harker.

options.outcome: Dr Seward leads you down a corridor that smells of carbolic. You are warned not to give the man anything sharp. The attendant has a stout stick and does not take his eyes off the door.

echoes.text: Jonathan's journal goes into the Professor's hands with the wax still on it.
The bruise in the crook of your arm has gone yellow.
Arthur drove the stake himself. He thanks you with his eyes whenever he sees you.
You have the empty coffin's measurements in your notebook.
You have seen what Lucy became in the tomb. You have put it in the record, and not in the words you would use aloud.

2-DARK.title: The Figure on the Abbey Steps
2-DARK.description: The coastguard's lantern is out of oil by the time you leave the harbour office, and the fog has followed you up the hill. At the turn of the hundred and ninety-nine steps a tall, thin man stands with his back to the wall. He wears dark clothes and he is very pale. He is not looking at you. He is looking up at the lit window on the crescent where Lucy is brushing her hair. When the lamp gutters, the step is empty.

options.label: Stay where you are and watch the window.
options.detail: You are not sure he is real. You would like to see what he does.

quote.speaker: Your journal
quote.text: I could not have moved if I had tried. So I wrote down what I saw.

options.outcome: You hold the rail until the church clock strikes. Nothing comes down the stairs. In your notebook, in shorthand, you set down his height, his coat and the way the light did not seem to touch his face. You do not tell Lucy.

options.label: Hurry home and bolt the doors.
options.detail: A man below a young woman's window is a matter for the police, and the police are at the pier.

quote.speaker: Lucy
quote.text: You are white as the sheet, Mina. Was somebody on the stairs?

options.outcome: You bolt the front door and the area door, and look to the windows, and tell Lucy it was the fog. She looks at you for some time and does not believe you.

options.label: Raise the lantern and call out to him.
options.detail: You are not afraid of a thin man in a long coat. You are a schoolmistress, and you have faced worse in a back row.

quote.speaker: Mina
quote.text: I said, who is there? And he turned, as if I had called him by his name.

success.outcome: He turns. For the length of a breath you see his face, and his eyes take the lamp and give it back red. Then he steps backward into the fog and is not there. You find that you are not afraid, and that this is the part you will not be able to explain.

failure.outcome: The lantern goes out in your hand. When you have found a match there is a smell of wet earth on the step and nothing else. Something has touched your wrist. The skin is cold and slightly raised, like a nettle sting.

4-HOME.title: Jonathan Comes Home
4-HOME.description: The clerk brings Jonathan to Hillingham on the third Friday in August. He has lost two stones and his hair has gone white. He knows you, and weeps on the doorstep, and Mrs Westenra, who has never met him, takes him for a patient and fusses over him. In the hall he presses a small book into your hands, tied with ribbon and sealed with wax, and asks you not to open it unless some solemn duty requires it. He wants to marry you quickly, at the parish church. Upstairs, Lucy is asleep in the afternoon again.

options.label: Marry him in the parish church, with the journal unopened.
options.detail: He asked you not to read it. Lucy will be your bridesmaid if she can stand.

quote.speaker: Jonathan
quote.text: I have been a long way from you, Mina. Put the book away, and do not look at it.

options.outcome: Lucy comes to the church in a borrowed hat and holds your flowers with both hands. The register is signed in the vestry by a clerk who is plainly trying not to stare at the groom's hair. The book goes into the bottom of your trunk, with the wax unbroken.

options.label: Read the journal that night, while he sleeps.
options.detail: You have nursed one sick person this month and you will not nurse another in the dark.

quote.speaker: Jonathan's journal
quote.text: I write this in shorthand because I will not have it read by anyone who has not been where I have been.

options.outcome: You read the whole of it at the table in the boarding-room, with the door shut. In it there are a castle, a count, three women, and a wall that a man climbs like a lizard. You close the book at dawn. You marry Jonathan on Saturday and say nothing.

options.label: Ask the clerk what he saw on the road from Buda-Pesth.
options.detail: Men tell a clerk things in a railway carriage that they will not tell a wife.

quote.speaker: The clerk
quote.text: He woke at every station, ma'am, and asked the porter whether anyone had a box. A large box. He would not say what sort.

options.outcome: The clerk is uncomfortable and sets it down in a list: the nights, the shouting, the box. He says Mr Harker asked at every station whether there had been a coffin among the freight. You are married on Saturday. The box is on your mind at the altar.

6-VIGIL.title: The Tomb at Kingstead
6-VIGIL.description: Lucy is buried on a Saturday, in the family tomb at Kingstead. Ten days later the newspapers carry a story about children found on the Heath at night, with small marks at their throats, who say that a tall lady in white took them for a walk. The papers call her the Bloofer Lady. The Professor puts the cuttings on Dr Seward's desk without a word. Then he says that on the next dark night he must open the tomb, and that Arthur must be told, and that someone should go with him who will not faint.

options.label: Go to the tomb with the men, and see for yourself.
options.detail: You have seen worse than a vault this month, and you would rather not be told about it afterwards.

quote.speaker: Van Helsing
quote.text: Madam Mina, you are a brave woman. I wish that I could say there is nothing in that tomb to be brave about.

options.outcome: The coffin is empty. The lead is cut like paper and the satin lining is stained. At two in the morning she comes across the grass in her white shroud with a child in her arms, and she is not Lucy. The Professor lifts his crucifix. She drops the child. Arthur, beside you, makes a sound you will not forget.

options.label: Take Arthur aside first, and prepare him for what he is to do.
options.detail: He will be asked to put a stake through the woman he married in his heart. He should not be asked in front of strangers.

quote.speaker: Arthur
quote.text: If it is her, Mina, I would rather it were my hand than another's. Tell me how it is done.

options.outcome: You walk with Arthur by the river for an hour. He cries once and says nothing else for a long time. At the end he nods. He is the one who drives the stake that night, with the Professor's hand beside his, and he does it cleanly. You are not in the tomb. You are at the gate with the lantern.

options.label: Insist on seeing the empty coffin by daylight before anyone does anything else.
options.detail: You have read Seward's notes and the Professor's theory. You want one thing you can put in a report.

quote.speaker: Dr Seward
quote.text: Mrs Harker is right. If we are going to do this, we ought to be sure of the coffin first.

options.outcome: The sexton opens the tomb at noon with a crowbar and a look of dislike. Lucy's coffin is empty. You make notes in shorthand, as you would at an inquest, and the Professor says that this is the first time anyone has taken a vampire's measurements with a tape. That night the work is done by men who have seen the evidence for themselves.

echoes.text: Arthur has not forgotten that you were the one who told him, on the platform.

7-ASYLUM.title: Renfield's Room
7-ASYLUM.description: The patient is a stout, pale man of about fifty with a heavy jaw and a tidy room. He is sitting on the edge of his bed with a small box on his knee. In the box is a spider, and he feeds it a fly, very gently. He looks at you for a long time and then says that you smell of the sea, and that the Master has been at your window. His voice is quite reasonable. He says that he is sorry for what he must do when the Master calls him, and that he would like to ask you to be kind to his flies.

options.label: Be kind to him, and ask what the Master wants.
options.detail: A man who is sorry is not entirely lost. He may tell you something useful out of gratitude.

quote.speaker: Renfield
quote.text: He wants the house. He wants all of you. He wants me to open the door. I do not wish to open the door, Mrs Harker.

options.outcome: He answers you in sentences that run straight and then double back on themselves. At the end he asks you for a kitten. You say that you cannot. He says that he understands, and that he is sorry about the door. Dr Seward writes it all down on his cuff.

options.label: Ask him straight out whether he has let the Count in.
options.detail: You have not the time for tact and he is the only person who knows.

quote.speaker: Renfield
quote.text: I am a madman, Mrs Harker. Madmen are never asked such questions. I shall say that I have not, and you must decide whether to believe it.

options.outcome: His face changes at the word. For a moment you see a man, frightened and ashamed, and then the other voice takes over. He rocks on the bed and will not look at you. As you leave he whispers that the door is not locked, and the attendant tells you that this is what he says every night.

options.label: Leave a note, and step back from the door.
options.detail: He is not safe, and you are the only one who has seen him not be mad. Let him see it written down.

quote.speaker: Dr Seward
quote.text: I think that was wise. Mrs Harker, you should not see him again alone.

options.outcome: You write a plain note in shorthand and push it under the door: that you are sorry, that he is not alone, that there are people who mean to fight. He reads it aloud twice. He says it is very kind. When you have gone, the attendant hears him crying.

7-COUNCIL.title: The Council, Again
7-COUNCIL.description: You come back to the study with the smell of carbolic still on your sleeve. Nobody has moved. The Professor has not slept, and Quincey has been cleaning his rifle on a newspaper for an hour. They look at you as you sit down, and Dr Seward repeats what Renfield said, as nearly as he can, in his flat professional voice. The Count has a way into the asylum, and the way is a man who does not want to open the door. The Professor looks round the table once more and asks again for a plan.

options.label: Follow the Professor's way: find the boxes and make them unfit for him with the Host and the rite.
options.detail: The boxes are his ground. Take away the ground, and he has nowhere to lie by day.

quote.speaker: Van Helsing
quote.text: Each box we sanctify is a door we close. He has fifty doors. We have a little bread, and a great deal of patience.

options.outcome: The room agrees, Quincey Morris with a drawl and Arthur with a nod. Jonathan watches you rather than the Professor. You say that you will keep the record of every box that is closed, and Van Helsing says that is the most useful thing anyone has offered yet.

options.label: Follow the paper: trace the boxes through the solicitor, the carters and the railway.
options.detail: Fifty boxes do not move themselves. Somebody drove a cart, and somebody signed for them.

quote.speaker: Jonathan
quote.text: Billington and Son took the delivery at Whitby. Carter, Paterson and Company carted it to Purfleet. A man who leaves a trail of receipts can be found.

options.outcome: Jonathan takes up the idea as if it were a drink of water. By noon he has a list of names, and you have sorted it into a table, and Quincey has put a pin in a map of London for every house that has had a delivery from Whitby. The Professor says that he is a very old man and has never been so pleased to be shown a timetable.

options.label: Tell them about the dreams, and ask the Professor to put you under.
options.detail: Since Whitby you have dreamed of the sea at night, and of a voice. If the Count can see you, you may be able to see him.

quote.speaker: Van Helsing
quote.text: Madam Mina, you are offering me a window into the enemy's house. I do not like it. I am going to accept.

options.outcome: Jonathan stands up, then sits down again. Dr Seward says it is unwise. Arthur says that he would rather it were him. The Professor says it cannot be done with anyone else, and that if Mrs Harker is certain he will not forbid her. You say that you are certain. You are not, but you are the only person in the room who has been looked at by him.

echoes.text: Renfield told you the door was not locked. Dr Seward has had the lock changed twice since.

8A.title: Twenty-Nine Boxes at Carfax
8A.description: Carfax is a damp old house with a ruined chapel at the end of the grounds. Inside the chapel, among fallen plaster and rat droppings, the hunters count twenty-nine wooden boxes. Each is heavy, and each smells of earth that is not English. Rats go out between your feet. On a tombstone the Professor lays out his case: crucifixes, a bundle of wild rose, and a small silver box of Host, consecrated in Amsterdam, of which he has brought as many as he dared. He says there is enough for the work in London if the work is done sparingly. The Professor does not say how sparingly that is.

options.label: Lay a piece of the Host in every box and close the lids.
options.detail: It is the plain rite, and it is quick. It uses most of what the Professor carries.

quote.speaker: Van Helsing
quote.text: Lay it in the earth, so. Now he cannot rest in this one. Say the words and mean them.

options.outcome: You lay the wafer in the dirt, the Professor says the words, and then the next, and the next. Twenty-nine times. When it is done the chapel is colder and the rats do not come back. The silver box is nearly empty.

options.label: Seal all twenty-nine, but keep a third of the Host back.
options.detail: There are other houses, and there is your own bed. A rite that runs out in London is a rite wasted.

quote.speaker: Quincey
quote.text: You keep a little powder dry, Doc. That is all Mrs Harker is saying, and I second it.

options.outcome: The Professor argues for a minute and gives in. Twenty boxes are sealed whole. Nine are closed with a cross scratched in the lid and a thinner measure of the Host. "It is a risk," he says, "and it is yours." He writes the numbers of the nine in his notebook.

options.label: Sit up in the chapel with Quincey and let the Count come back to his boxes.
options.detail: A hunter who waits in the dark may finish the quarry sooner than one who chases it.

quote.speaker: Quincey
quote.text: I have sat up for a mountain lion for three nights, ma'am. This does not seem much worse.

success.outcome: At dusk the rats come in a body and go back out again. Something tall stands in the chapel door against the last light. Quincey's rifle comes up. The Professor's crucifix comes up. It looks at the boxes, at you, at the Host in the Professor's hand, and then it is not in the door. You have seen him, and he has seen you. Quincey says quietly that being afraid does not trouble him. He would like it to be some use.

failure.outcome: The Count does not come. The rats do, in thousands, out of the walls and the floor, and Quincey empties both barrels before you leave. Your ankle has been bitten through the stocking, and in the morning the Professor burns the dressing in the grate without telling you why.

9A.title: The Houses in Piccadilly and the East End
9A.description: Jonathan's papers give three more addresses. One is a tall house in Piccadilly with its blinds down. The others are a warehouse yard at Mile End and a decayed court in Bermondsey. The Professor wants all three closed before the Count can use them. He divides the party over breakfast. Lord Godalming can open a door in the West End by being himself. Quincey can walk the East End in daylight without being noticed. The asylum needs a person at the telegraph, and somebody has to watch the house next door.

options.label: Go with Arthur to Piccadilly, and use his name and a locksmith.
options.detail: Lord Godalming can open any door in London if he is seen to own it.

quote.speaker: Arthur
quote.text: I shall say I am the new owner and I am anxious about the drains. One does not ask a lord to prove he owns a drain.

options.outcome: Arthur plays the new owner, and a locksmith who is paid by the hour and has no questions opens the cellar. There are nine boxes. The Professor speaks the words over each and closes the lids. The locksmith asks whether the house will be sold. Arthur says certainly, and tips him twice what he is owed.

options.label: Walk the Mile End and Bermondsey addresses with Quincey.
options.detail: Slums, a canal, and cabmen who remember a customer with an odd accent.

quote.speaker: Quincey
quote.text: Stay on the pavement side of me, ma'am, and if anyone asks, you are my cousin who is going blind.

options.outcome: The Mile End yard has a door that has not been painted in ten years and a landlord who has not been paid in eight. In Bermondsey a child tells you that "a gentleman with the long teeth" goes in and out at night. You seal what you find, six boxes at Mile End and six at Bermondsey, and you go home with your hem black to the knee.

options.label: Stay at the asylum with the telegraph and the records.
options.detail: Somebody has to be at the end of the wire, and the Count's house is next door.

quote.speaker: Dr Seward
quote.text: I should be glad of you, Mrs Harker. Renfield is much worse and I have forty pages to make fair copies of.

options.outcome: You spend the day with the typewriter and the telegraph, copying the Professor's dictation and Seward's cylinders and the replies that come in from Billington's and the carters. By nightfall you have a map of which houses have been dealt with and which have not. It is a long afternoon, and a quiet one.

options.label: Pay a cabby and a locksmith to keep their mouths shut, and have the whole round done in a day.
options.detail: It is expensive, and it is fast, and the Count may hear of it.

quote.speaker: Locksmith
quote.text: I do not know what is in the boxes, sir, and the price is for me not knowing it.

options.outcome: By evening all three houses are sealed and twenty-one more boxes are closed. The cabby is thanked with a sovereign. The locksmith shakes your hand with a face that says he will talk about this for forty years in a public house.

10A.title: The Night Visit
10A.description: At one in the morning the attendant finds Renfield on the floor of his room with his head broken. Upstairs, your own door is locked from the inside. The men put it in with a shoulder. You are on the bed. Jonathan lies beside you in a stupor, not asleep and not awake. A tall man in black stands over you with one hand on the back of your neck, and there is a cut on his chest, and a thread of blood on his shirt, and he has been making you drink. Candles, crosses and Host come up in the doorway at the length of five arms. He lets you go. He looks at them for the space of a breath, and then he is a mist under the door.

options.label: Hold out your forehead for the Host, and let the Professor touch it.
options.detail: You are not sure what you are. The Professor is, and he is willing to be wrong.

quote.speaker: Van Helsing
quote.text: Courage, Madam Mina. This will hurt. I am sorry for it. Hold still.

options.outcome: The wafer touches your skin with a hiss like a drop of water on a hot iron. You cry out and cover your face. When you take your hands down there is a red mark on your forehead, the size of a coin. Jonathan, awake at last, puts his arms round you. Nobody looks away.

options.label: Refuse the Host. Ask them to give you one night to think.
options.detail: You are afraid of what the answer might be, and you want to be yourself a little longer.

quote.speaker: Mina
quote.text: I know what I am afraid of. Please, not tonight. Let me be myself a little longer.

options.outcome: The Professor lowers the wafer. The men look at each other, and no one argues. You sit with a shawl round you and your hands in your lap. There is a pressure behind your eyes, like someone listening. You say nothing of it.

options.label: Say your own name to him, and refuse him.
options.detail: It is a mad idea. It is the only thing in the room that belongs to you.

quote.speaker: Mina
quote.text: I said it as I would say it to a stranger in a railway carriage. Wilhelmina Murray. And he heard.

success.outcome: You say your name aloud and his hand loosens. For a second you are more afraid of his surprise than of him. Then the door goes in. Afterwards the Professor will say that he has never seen a woman do that, and that he does not mean to see another do it twice.

failure.outcome: You say the words and nothing follows them. His hand tightens. The door breaks while you are still gasping. In the morning your mouth is raw, and you know, without being told, how much of him you swallowed.

echoes.text: You had seen his face once already, in the chapel door. It is the same face. It is more tired than you expected.
Your record of the sealed houses is on the desk where the Professor can find it.

11A.title: The Council You Are Not Asked To
11A.description: At breakfast Jonathan will not look at you. The men met in the study before you were up, and Dr Seward comes out with the pained courtesy of a man who has been told to speak for the committee. They have decided, for your safety, to tell you nothing of their plans. If the Count can reach your mind, he can read what is in it. The Professor sits in his chair by the window, looking old, and says nothing at all.

options.label: Accept it. You see the sense, and you are tired.
options.detail: A woman who has been bitten may do more harm by knowing than by being kept in ignorance.

quote.speaker: Jonathan
quote.text: You are very good about it, Mina. I could not have borne an argument.

options.outcome: You go to your room and sleep for eleven hours. When you wake it is dark and the house is quiet, and you know by the shape of the quiet that something has been decided without you.

options.label: Refuse. Say plainly that you will not be left in the dark again.
options.detail: You have typed every page of this. You will not be handed the ending as a parcel.

quote.speaker: Mina
quote.text: I will not be put in a drawer like the good china. You will tell me everything, or I shall find it out.

options.outcome: The Professor takes off his glasses and rubs his eyes. He says that Madam Mina is right, and the committee is a fool, and he will say so in Latin if necessary. The vote is taken again. This time it is five to nothing, and Jonathan's is the loudest.

options.label: Agree, on one condition: that you keep the record and know the outline.
options.detail: The hour of striking can be kept in the Professor's pocket. The plan cannot be kept from the person who has been typing it.

quote.speaker: Van Helsing
quote.text: A bargain. You will know the road, and the hour we keep in the pocket. It is fair.

options.outcome: It takes ten minutes. Dr Seward is the last to sign the minute, and he does it as if the pen were hot. You keep the record, you know the road, and the hour is never spoken aloud in front of you.

echoes.text: The mark on your forehead has begun to scab. The Professor changes the dressing himself every evening and does not look at it for long.
You did not take the Host. It has not been mentioned since, which is its own way of mentioning it.
Piccadilly and the East End are sealed. The Count has fewer doors than he had.
You said your name and he heard it. The men look at you as if they are not sure how to ask.
The taste of him is still in your mouth. You have not told anyone what you swallowed.

12A.title: The Czarina Catherine
12A.description: The Professor counts forty-nine boxes sealed and one gone. A telegram from Lloyd's says that a steamer, the Czarina Catherine, has sailed for Varna with a single large box among her cargo, marked for a forwarding agent at Galatz. The Count is going home. The Professor says there is a train, a boat and another train, and that if the party leaves tonight, it can be in Varna before the steamer. He puts the matter to the table. He does not say that he expects it to be easy.

options.label: Go by rail to Varna with the Professor.
options.detail: It is quick, and the Professor will want you where he can see you.

quote.speaker: Van Helsing
quote.text: We leave by the Dover boat at ten, Madam Mina. Bring a warm cloak and a small bag. A very small bag.

options.outcome: The Professor buys the tickets. You are on the boat train before eleven, with the Host in the Professor's coat and your typewriter in your hand. The others will follow by different ways. Jonathan kisses you on the platform and says nothing, and he keeps looking at the mark on your forehead and away.

options.label: Go by sea with Jonathan and Arthur, in a hired steam launch.
options.detail: Arthur can pay, and the launch can follow the steamer through the Straits.

quote.speaker: Arthur
quote.text: I have never owned a boat before. I find I am looking forward to it.

options.outcome: The launch is called the Zenobia and she makes thirteen knots in a flat sea. You are sick for two days and then not, and you spend the third on the deck with a rug round your knees, copying the Professor's last notes. Jonathan keeps a watch. Arthur stands the night with a boathook and a rifle across his arm.

options.label: Insist on travelling with the whole party, by rail, and leave the Zenobia to the others.
options.detail: A party that arrives together has a better chance of leaving together.

quote.speaker: Jonathan
quote.text: I should like us to be in the same railway carriage, Mina. Whatever we find, I should like to have been there.

options.outcome: The Professor looks at you for a moment and says that a single word from you is worth three orders from him. Six people travel in two second-class compartments through France. Quincey sleeps with his boots on. Arthur snores. At the frontier you sit awake with the Professor and a flask of tea, and he tells you why he came to England.

echoes.text: You were not at the table when this was decided. Dr Seward gives you the minute afterwards, and you read it on the stairs.
The Professor now asks your opinion first. He pretends it is a courtesy.
You know the road and the Professor holds the hour.

13A.title: Varna
13A.description: Varna is white with heat and loud with gulls. The harbour master says that the Czarina Catherine is not yet in. The agent at Galatz has wired, and so has a man named Hildesheim, who deals in forwarding and claims to be anxious for a large box. The Professor stands on the quay with his hat pulled over his eyes. Somewhere in the Black Sea, in a closed hold, a box of earth, heavy as a man, is lying on its side with a man in it. There is a priest's house behind the church, and an Orthodox chapel that has stood at the harbour since the Turks.

options.label: Go to the Orthodox priest and ask for his blessing on the Host.
options.detail: The Professor's Host is Catholic. The priest is not. A second blessing does no harm and may do good.

quote.speaker: Priest
quote.text: I do not know what you carry. My grandmother would have known. I bless it as she would have.

options.outcome: He listens without surprise, which surprises you. He blesses the Host with a long prayer in Slavonic, and when he is done, he gives you wild roses from his own garden and a small iron cross on a thong. The Professor says that the rite is in better hands than his.

options.label: Wait on the quay with the Host in your pocket and watch every box that comes ashore.
options.detail: He has to land somewhere. He will be in the hold until dark.

quote.speaker: Quincey
quote.text: I have watched cattle cars come in for three days at a time. A man gets a feel for them.

options.outcome: You stand in the sun for two days. A great many boxes come ashore, and not one has a coat of arms on it. When the Czarina Catherine finally comes in, the hold is empty. The box was lifted off at sea by a small boat before she entered port.

options.label: Board the Czarina Catherine the moment she docks, and go down into her hold with the Host.
options.detail: The Count is in a box in the dark and cannot move until dusk. This is the one time he cannot stop you.

quote.speaker: Van Helsing
quote.text: If he is in the hold, he is in the earth, and if he is in the earth he is mine until sunset.

success.outcome: The captain is fond of bribes and slow to see them as an insult. The hold is hot and black, and the box has been moved. Where it stood is a patch of earth on the planks, dry and fresh. The Professor lays a wafer in it and says the words, so that the Count cannot come back to the ship.

failure.outcome: The captain is plainly told what the hold contains, and plainly decides not to believe it. You are shown off the ship by two sailors who do not touch you. The Professor mutters in Dutch all the way down the gangway, and you notice that he does not cross himself.

echoes.text: Arthur and Jonathan are still on the water. You and the Professor are first to arrive and have only the gulls to talk to.
The Zenobia put in to Varna that morning with salt in her rigging. Arthur was grey and delighted.
All six of you are on the quay together, which is more than anyone expected.

14A.title: The Circle on the Pass
14A.description: The box has been lifted from the steamer and put on a river barge bound for the mountains. You reach the Borgo Pass at dusk on the seventh day, with a dozen men from the villages and two waggons. The Professor chooses a flat place under a rock. He lays a ring of Host in the grass around you, as wide as a room, and tells you that on no account must you leave it between dusk and dawn. The horses scream. Wolves come out of the dark in a ring of their own. Three pale women stand at the edge of the Host, laughing, and one of them holds out her arms and says your name.

options.label: Stay in the circle, and shut your eyes.
options.detail: The Host will hold. The Professor said so. Believe it as if it were arithmetic.

quote.speaker: Van Helsing
quote.text: Do not look at them, Madam Mina. They are very beautiful, and that is the whole of their argument.

options.outcome: You sit in the ring with your hands over your ears and recite the multiplication tables. Beyond the Host the wolves wait. The women talk, and sing, and laugh, and one weeps. At dawn the ring is unbroken and the grass outside it is trampled flat.

options.label: Speak to them from inside the ring, and ask what they want.
options.detail: If they will not speak truly, they at least cannot lie about what they are.

quote.speaker: Bride
quote.text: We want what he wants, little sister. We want you with us. We want you never to be tired again.

options.outcome: You ask them questions through the night. The tallest answers you for hours. She says she was a girl in a village three hundred years ago, and that she had a sister, and that it hurt less than you would think. In the morning the Professor looks at your face and gives you tea without saying anything.

options.label: Pray aloud for the length of the night, with the Professor and the iron cross.
options.detail: You do not know what is listening. You know that the Professor believes someone is.

quote.speaker: Van Helsing
quote.text: Say the Our Father with me, and then the Hail Mary, and then whatever you have left. We have until dawn.

options.outcome: You say every prayer you were taught and several that you were not. The Professor says them in Latin and Dutch and a little Hebrew. By the third hour the women have stopped laughing. By the fifth they have stopped coming near. At dawn there is frost on the Host, and none on you.

echoes.text: The wild rose from the priest at Varna lies under the Host in the grass. The wolves keep clear of that side of the ring.
You count the wafers in the Professor's silver box. There are just enough to make the circle, and none beyond it.
The officer at Varna believes you are chasing a missing coffin. A pamphlet on the history of the port is in the Professor's pocket.
A sovereign at the customs house bought you twenty minutes. The Professor says it was the best rite of the day.
The Professor has a black eye from the customs house. He wears it as if it were a decoration.
The ship's hold has been sealed. He cannot go back to it.
Two days on the quay have burnt your face. Not a word is said.

15A.title: Sunset at the Pass
15A.description: A little before sunset on the third day the waggons come round the bend of the road with the gipsies on the box and the great box of earth in the bed of the second. The sun is lying along the rim of the pass. Jonathan is on the near side with his long knife and Quincey on the far side with his, and the Professor is on the rock above, holding the Host in one hand and the cross in the other. Arthur has the horses. You are in the circle with a rifle you do not know how to use. In a very few minutes the sun will touch the ridge, and the lid of the box will lift.

options.label: Let the men strike: the long knife at the throat and the bowie at the heart, as the light goes.
options.detail: It is what the others came for, and the sun is on your side for eleven more minutes.

quote.speaker: Quincey
quote.text: Mr Harker, you take the throat. I will see to the heart. Ma'am, you keep behind the Doc.

options.outcome: The lid goes back and the face inside is pale and open-eyed. The long knife goes across the throat and the bowie goes into the heart. The Count crumbles to dust in a breath, and the dust is gone before it settles. Quincey's side has been cut, and he leans against the box, smiling. "I am glad," he says. "Look, ma'am."

options.label: Say the burial office over the box, and ask the men to wait until you finish.
options.detail: He has been dead for four hundred years. Somebody should say it aloud.

quote.speaker: Van Helsing
quote.text: Madam Mina, there is not time. But if there were time, I would choose this. Say it. We will hold the road.

options.outcome: You read the words from the Professor's prayer-book with the rifle across your knees, in a voice that the wind carries. Jonathan holds the horses. The room is silent. When you come to the committal you hear the lid lift, and a voice in the box says a single word, and it is not a curse.

options.label: Close the box with the last of the Host, seal the lid with iron, and carry it down to the church.
options.detail: A box that cannot be opened cannot be harmed by daylight or by moonlight, and it does not need to be killed to be stopped.

quote.speaker: Van Helsing
quote.text: A box of iron and Host, buried in holy ground, and a priest with a key. It is a very old way. It is not a cheap one.

options.outcome: You fix the Host under the lid and run the iron bands round it, one after another, while the others hold the gipsies at bay with rifles. The box is hauled down to the village on a sledge. The priest is woken at midnight. By morning it is in the crypt of the church, under three feet of stone.
options.requiresFlagHint: NEEDS HOST KEPT IN RESERVE AT CARFAX

options.label: Walk to the box alone and offer him what you can: the one rest he cannot take for himself.
options.detail: You have seen his face twice and each time it was tired.

quote.speaker: Mina
quote.text: You do not have to be this any longer. I think that you know it. I think that is what you wanted to ask.

options.outcome: The others lower their arms. You kneel at the box with your forehead near the lid, and you say what you came to say. There is a long silence. Then the Count's hand, which is white and long, comes out and touches your brow, and there is no heat in it. He looks at you with something that you can only call relief, and then the sun is gone behind the ridge and he is dust.
options.requiresHint: OPENS TO WHAT YOUR EARLIER MERCIES AND FAITH HAVE MADE YOU

echoes.text: The mark on your forehead aches in the cold. It has ached since the beginning of the climb.
You can still say every prayer you said last night. You are not sure whether you want to.

8B.title: The Paper Trail
8B.description: By eight in the morning the study is a counting-house. Jonathan has the delivery book from Billington and Son. Quincey has a map of London with a pin for every house that has had a cart from Whitby. Dr Seward has a friend at Carter, Paterson and Company, who has a cousin on the railway. The Professor sits in a corner with the Host in his lap, trying not to look like a man who believes in a different kind of arithmetic. You have your typewriter, a ream of paper, and a telegraph form for every port on the Thames.

options.label: Type up the table of boxes: where each was delivered, by whom, and when.
options.detail: Sort the deliveries into one table that every man in the room can read at once.

quote.speaker: Jonathan
quote.text: Number the boxes, Mina. Put the carter's name beside each. If one is missing, I want to see it on the page.

options.outcome: By noon you have a typed schedule of fifty entries with columns for the date, the carter, the house and the cellar. Dr Seward reads it with the expression of a man who has found the doctor's handwriting legible for once. Quincey takes it to the wall and pins it up.

options.label: Send a wire to every port agent and shipping office on the Thames.
options.detail: If the Count means to leave, he will have to be put on a ship, and every ship has a clerk.

quote.speaker: Dr Seward
quote.text: The telegraph clerk at Purfleet says he has not been so busy since the Jubilee. He is charging us for each word.

options.outcome: You write twenty-six wires, each two lines long, asking after a single large box, consigned to a Galatz agent, loaded in the last week. By evening you have eleven answers. Nine say no. Two say they will look into it, and one of those adds that it is not in the habit of being asked.

options.label: Hire an inquiry agent to follow the carters, and pay him out of Arthur's account.
options.detail: An agent can watch the carters' street for a week and be forgotten.

quote.speaker: Arthur
quote.text: I do not mind what it costs. I mind what it does not buy.

options.outcome: The agent is a plump, quiet person with a notebook. He asks for ten pounds in advance and does not ask what the boxes contain. In two days he finds three carters who remember the loads, and a boy who saw a tall man with a white moustache at Piccadilly at three in the morning.

9B.title: The Carters and the Cabmen
9B.description: The paper gives you the houses. It does not give you the people who carried the boxes, and those are the ones who will have seen the Count. A carter at Carter, Paterson's remembers a gentleman in a long coat who tipped well and who did not seem to eat. A cabman at Piccadilly remembers a man with a white moustache who had a way of not being there when the door opened. Quincey wants to put a rifle on every corner. The Professor wants the Host in every cellar. Jonathan wants a list.

options.label: Meet the carrier's man yourself, in a tea-shop, and ask what he saw.
options.detail: A schoolmistress with a notebook is the least alarming person in London.

quote.speaker: Carter
quote.text: He tipped a sovereign for a half-day's work, miss, and he looked like he had not slept in a hundred years.

success.outcome: He talks for forty minutes and eats four buns. The gentleman paid in gold, and the gold was old, and the carter kept one coin. He shows it to you. It is a Hungarian ducat of a century you have never studied. You take a rubbing of it in your notebook, and the Professor will treasure it.

failure.outcome: He answers questions about the gentleman with great politeness and no detail. Somebody has been here before you. The boy at the counter says that an elderly foreigner left a sovereign for the carter this morning and said nothing at all.

options.label: Go with Quincey to Piccadilly at night, and watch the house from a doorway.
options.detail: The cabmen are right that something goes in and out. You would like to see it.

quote.speaker: Quincey
quote.text: Keep your head down, ma'am. If anything comes out of that door that is not a policeman, say so quiet.

options.outcome: At half past two a tall man comes up the area steps with a box on his shoulder that no man could carry. He sets it in a cab. The cab goes towards the river. Quincey takes a shot at the tyres and misses. You have the number of the cab, and the time, and a wet hem.

options.label: Stay at the desk and cross-check the carters against Seward's cylinders.
options.detail: Somebody must find the pattern, and the pattern is in the dates.

quote.speaker: Dr Seward
quote.text: Mrs Harker, I should say that you are the only one of us whose arithmetic I trust.

options.outcome: By dusk you have found that the boxes were moved on nights with no moon, and that three deliveries are missing from Billington's book. You write all of it up. It is the dullest document in the case, and Jonathan says it is the best.

10B.title: The Night Visit, Written Down
10B.description: Renfield is found on the floor of his room at one in the morning with his head broken. Upstairs your own door is locked from the inside. The men put it in with a shoulder. You are on the bed. Jonathan lies beside you in a stupor, not asleep and not awake. A tall man in black stands over you with a hand at the back of your neck, and there is a cut on his chest, and he has been making you drink. Candles and crosses come up in the doorway. He lets you go. He looks at the men for the space of a breath, and then he is a mist under the door.

options.label: Let Dr Seward dress the wound and give you something to sleep.
options.detail: You will do no good to anyone with your hands shaking. Sleep, then the day's work.

quote.speaker: Dr Seward
quote.text: A grain of chloral, Mrs Harker, and nothing more. I shall sit by the bed. I am afraid I am no use at all at anything else.

options.outcome: The draught is bitter. Dr Seward sits by the bed with his notebook and does not write anything. You sleep for ten hours and dream of the sea. When you wake, someone has left a bunch of snowdrops on the table, which is impossible in October, and the house will not say who.

options.label: Refuse the draught. Sit up with Jonathan, the lamp lit and a revolver in your lap.
options.detail: You do not intend to be asleep when it comes back.

quote.speaker: Jonathan
quote.text: You do not know how to fire that, Mina. Put it down, please. It is making me nervous.

options.outcome: You sit up all night. The lamp burns down and you trim it. The revolver is heavy and you do not know how to use it. At dawn Jonathan wakes with a start, sees you, and weeps. Neither of you says what is the matter. Neither of you needs to.

options.label: Write down everything now, in shorthand, while it is fresh.
options.detail: In a week it will have changed in the telling, and a record that has changed is not a record.

quote.speaker: Mina
quote.text: I made the entry before I washed my face. I think the others thought it was shock. It was method.

options.outcome: You set it down by lamplight, in a shorthand the house cannot read: the hand at your neck, the cut, the way the candles did not flicker. When you finish you read it back and it looks like a medical history. The Professor will say later that it is the best account of the first night he has ever seen.

echoes.text: The carter's Hungarian ducat is in your pocket-book. The Professor handles the rubbing as if it were a relic.
The number of the cab is in your notebook, with the time, written in a hand that is not quite steady.

11B.title: The Committee
11B.description: At breakfast Jonathan will not look at you. The men met in the study before you were up, and Dr Seward comes out with the pained courtesy of a man who has been told to speak for the committee. They have decided, for your safety, to tell you nothing of their plans. If the Count can reach your mind, he can read what is in it. The Professor sits by the window and says nothing. On the desk there is a pile of paper which you recognise as yours: your table, your timetable, your notes. They have all been read.

options.label: Accept the decision. Offer the table as a gift and go and lie down.
options.detail: Leave the typescript with them and go to bed. You are tired.

quote.speaker: Jonathan
quote.text: You are very good about it, Mina. I could not have borne an argument.

options.outcome: You leave the typescript on the desk and go to your room. It is the best thing you have ever typed, and you do not think you will see it again. Through the wall you hear the men reading it out loud, and then a long silence.

options.label: Refuse. Put your timetable on the desk and ask them to tell you what is wrong with it.
options.detail: If they will not be told what they are doing wrong, they can be told what you have done right.

quote.speaker: Mina
quote.text: I have spent a week on this. If it is wrong, say so. If it is right, I should like to be consulted.

options.outcome: The Professor takes it up and reads it twice. He says that the table is correct to a quarter of an hour, and the committee is a fool, and he does not say it in Latin. Quincey lets out a breath and slaps his hat on his knee. The vote is five to nothing.

options.label: Agree on one condition: that you keep the record and the timetable.
options.detail: The hour of striking can be in the Professor's pocket. The railway guide cannot be anyone's but yours.

quote.speaker: Van Helsing
quote.text: A bargain. Madam Mina will keep the timetable and we shall keep the knives. It is a division of labour.

options.outcome: It takes ten minutes. Dr Seward writes the minute and signs it. The Professor, who has been quiet for an hour, says that it is a pleasure to be argued with by someone who has read the Bradshaw.

echoes.text: The chloral has left a flat grey taste in your mouth that no tea will shift.
You sat up all night with a revolver. It has not been mentioned, and Jonathan has put it away.
You said your name and he heard it. The men look at you as if they are not sure how to ask.

12B.title: The Time Tables
12B.description: Fifty boxes, and forty-nine sealed, burned or reported. The last has gone. The telegram from Lloyd's says it is on a steamer, the Czarina Catherine, bound for Varna. You spread the Bradshaw, the Continental Guide and a Lloyd's list across the desk. A rail party can be in Varna before the steamer if it leaves tonight. A launch could follow her through the Straits. The Professor says the party must divide, that every hour counts, and that Madam Mina has the arithmetic.

options.label: Draw up a strict timetable and send four parties by the four quickest routes.
options.detail: Everyone with a ticket, a wire and a time to reach a station.

quote.speaker: Jonathan
quote.text: I shall go by the Orient express with the Professor. Arthur by sea. Quincey and Seward by the Vienna road. And you, Mina, here at the telegraph.

options.outcome: By midnight the four parties have railway tickets, hotel addresses and a list of wires. You assign each man a day and a place, and your own part is to sit at the end of the telegraph and tell them where the others are. The Professor calls it the neatest operation order he has ever seen from an Englishwoman.

options.label: Buy a steam launch outright and send the three younger men after the ship.
options.detail: A launch can go where a train cannot, and Arthur can afford it.

quote.speaker: Arthur
quote.text: I have bought a steam launch. I did not ask the price. The man who sold her said she was lucky.

options.outcome: The launch is called the Zenobia and she is lying at Greenhithe with steam up. Arthur, Jonathan and Quincey leave on the evening tide with provisions for three weeks, two rifles and a barrel of coal. Dr Seward stays behind with the Professor. You are to go by rail.

options.label: Keep the whole party together on one train, and trust the Professor's judgment.
options.detail: A party that arrives together has a better chance of leaving together.

quote.speaker: Jonathan
quote.text: I should like us all to be in one carriage. Whatever we find, I would like to have been there.

options.outcome: Arthur pays for the tickets. You travel second class from Charing Cross with seven pieces of baggage, two Winchesters and a kukri in a violin case. Quincey sleeps with his boots on. At Cologne, Arthur buys a map and finds that the railway guide is wrong by a day.

echoes.text: You open the typescript at the page where the Czarina Catherine first appears. It is the only entry that the Professor has pencilled in the margin: a single question mark.
The Professor now asks your opinion first. He pretends it is a courtesy.

13B.title: Galatz
13B.description: The agent at Galatz has a reputation for never asking what a box holds. The Czarina Catherine has docked and gone on, and the box is already in a lighter on the river. The harbour is full of people who sell things and the quay is full of people who watch the people who sell things. You have a day, a telegraph, a purse, and a dozen letters of introduction. Jonathan has found a clerk at a forwarding agent's on the quay who says he will talk for a consideration. The Professor says that all things are to be had for a consideration, and that the trick is to pay in the right currency.

options.label: Wire the Lloyd's agent to hold the Czarina Catherine on a quarantine order.
options.detail: A false report of fever can hold a ship for a week, if the agent is persuaded to write it down.

quote.speaker: Lloyd's agent
quote.text: A case of cholera? Madam, I have had no case of cholera reported, and I am not in the habit of inventing one.

success.outcome: You do not say the word fever. You say that there are certain consignments that the Board of Trade has asked to be held for examination, and that the box is one. The agent looks at your wedding ring, at your typed credentials and at the Professor's visiting card, and takes a very long breath. The box is taken off the lighter and placed under seal in the customs shed at Galatz.

failure.outcome: The agent calls the chief clerk, who calls a policeman, who politely suggests that you leave the harbour. The box is on the river by dark. You have not been arrested. A man in a bowler hat has taken your name and the time.

options.label: Pay for the bill of lading, and for the agent's reply.
options.detail: A clerk costs less than a captain, and the paper is the same.

quote.speaker: Clerk
quote.text: It is not often that a lady comes to the office. For a lady, I make it fifteen. For the Professor I would make it twenty.

options.outcome: You come away with a copy of the bill of lading and the forwarding agent's letter: one large box, forty-four hundredweight, to go up the river and on by road to the Borgo Pass, in the care of a gang of Slovaks who have been paid in advance. The Professor reads it twice and says that the Count has been very careful and very stupid.

options.label: Go to the river and watch the quays with Quincey and a pair of field-glasses.
options.detail: Whatever he has paid for, the box must come ashore somewhere.

quote.speaker: Quincey
quote.text: I have seen a hundred barges and a thousand crates, and I can tell you that one is carrying more than his share.

options.outcome: You spend the afternoon on the roof of a grain store, looking through the glasses at the barges. At four a lighter moves out into the river with a box on its deck covered in tarpaulin. Quincey says nothing, but takes the glass and holds it a long time.

echoes.text: The four parties are in the field, and the wires from London arrive three times a day.
All six of you are on the quay together, which is more than anyone expected.

14B.title: The River Sereth
14B.description: The box has gone up the river on a barge with four Slovaks at the sweeps. The party has a steam launch, the one Arthur bought if you brought it, or one hired at Galatz for a price that Arthur does not discuss, and the chase begins at dawn. The river is brown and wide, and the banks are low and thick with willow. The barge is slow. It is also never in a straight line, and it hugs the shore wherever the water allows. Jonathan is on the bow with a rifle. Arthur is at the tiller. You are in the stern with a telegraph form, writing down the time of every bend.

options.label: Run the launch at full steam and try to get ahead of the barge.
options.detail: The river narrows beyond the next island. If you can pass her there, you can wait on the bank.

quote.speaker: Arthur
quote.text: She will give us fourteen knots if we ask nicely and twelve if we do not. I propose to ask nicely.

success.outcome: The launch lays herself over in the turn and goes through the narrows with the water breaking white. By noon you are three bends ahead of the barge. Quincey puts the rifle across his knees and looks at the trees. "There," he says. "That is a good spot to wait."

failure.outcome: A sandbar catches the keel. For two hours the launch cannot be moved, and the barge slides past a hundred yards away with the Slovaks looking back. Someone laughs. You fire a shot in the air, and the sound carries a long way.

options.label: Keep to the barge's pace and follow her at a distance, noting her stops.
options.detail: A barge that cannot be caught can be watched, and a barge that is watched can be met at the end.

quote.speaker: Jonathan
quote.text: He has to put in by dark. The Slovaks will not travel by night. Mark every landing, Mina, and the hour.

options.outcome: You note every landing, and the hour, and the number of men who go ashore. By evening you have a clear idea of her speed and of the next landing. Jonathan puts the glass down and says it is a relief to be doing a plain thing in a plain way.

options.label: Go ashore and ride ahead by road with Quincey, to reach the Pass first.
options.detail: The Count must come to the castle by the road. You can be there before him.

quote.speaker: Quincey
quote.text: A horse is a good thing. A rifle is a better one. Do you ride, ma'am?

options.outcome: You ride for six days on a borrowed pony and a worse saddle, with Quincey ahead and Dr Seward behind. You sleep in the stables of three villages. The wolves have come out early, and the farmers tell you that this is the sort of winter that makes people lock their doors.

echoes.text: The launch is yours. Arthur has stopped apologising for the price.
Behind you, in the customs shed, the box is under seal. The chase is a formality, whatever the others say.
You have the bill of lading in your pocket-book, with the route written on it.
You saw the barge go out. You know what it carries.

15B.title: The Wagon on the Road
15B.description: The box comes up out of the river on a waggon and goes up the road to the Pass with six Slovaks as escort and a clear sky above. It is three hours to sunset. The hunters have taken their places: Jonathan on the near bank with a long knife, Quincey on the far side with a Winchester, Arthur and Dr Seward with the horses, and the Professor on the hill above with the Host. You are in the cover of the trees with a typewriter, a rifle and a revolver, and a telegraph form on which you have written the time. If the box reaches the castle at dusk, the Count will rise and be home. If it does not, he will have to come out in the day.

options.label: Take the waggon in the open, in daylight, with the rifles ready and the knives at the box.
options.detail: The Slovaks will not fight for a stranger's box, and the sun is a good ally.

quote.speaker: Quincey
quote.text: Mr Harker, you take the throat and I will take the heart. Ma'am, you keep behind the trees.

options.outcome: The Slovaks scatter at the first shot. The lid comes off under two crowbars, and the face inside is pale and open-eyed, and in the sunlight it looks old. The long knife goes across the throat and the bowie goes into the heart. The Count crumbles to dust in a breath. Quincey, cut in the side, leans on the box and is smiling.

options.label: Sink the box in the river from the launch, with iron chains and a hundredweight of stones.
options.detail: Running water is the one thing he cannot cross, and a river is deep.

quote.speaker: Arthur
quote.text: I own a launch, a derrick, and four pounds of chain. I should like to see them used.

options.outcome: The launch comes alongside the barge in the dusk with a hawser and a hook, and four men heave the box over the side. It goes down with a sound like a door closing. Arthur lets out the chain. The river closes over it, and you stand on the deck and watch the ripples spread until there is only the water.
options.requiresFlagHint: NEEDS A LAUNCH OF YOUR OWN

options.label: Do not go to the Pass. Have the box opened under seal in the customs shed, at noon.
options.detail: A customs officer can open a box under seal, and the sun can reach a shed.

quote.speaker: Lloyd's agent
quote.text: The seal will be broken in the presence of two witnesses and the harbour master. You may attend, madam, if you do not touch anything.

options.outcome: The shed at Galatz is white with noon. Two officials, a clerk and the harbour master stand round a box that is no longer on the river. You watch the lid come up. There is a tall form in the earth, and a hand that closes on the edge, and then a sound like a long breath. The harbour master asks what the powder is. The clerk, writing, says that he supposes it is the packing.
options.requiresFlagHint: NEEDS THE BOX HELD UNDER SEAL AT GALATZ

options.label: Close the net: all four parties arrive at the same place, at the same hour, from four sides.
options.detail: You have the timetable and the wires. For once, everyone is where you wrote that they would be.

quote.speaker: Jonathan
quote.text: You said the fourteenth bridge at four fifteen. It is four fourteen, Mina. We are exactly on time.

options.outcome: At a quarter past four the waggon comes round the bend into a clearing where nine men, one woman and four horses are already waiting. The Slovaks lay down their knives. The box is opened and the thing inside has no time to rise.
options.requiresHint: NEEDS THE WIRES SENT, THE TIMETABLE KEPT, AND THE PARTY HOLDING TOGETHER

echoes.text: The Zenobia rides high without her stores. There is enough coal for a day and a half.
Your skirts have not dried since the sandbar, and you do not mind.
The farmer's rope is coiled in the stern. You have never owed anyone so little for so much.
You have the barge's landings in your book, and its speed to the quarter hour.
Your legs ache. You have not been on a horse for three years.
You have been waiting for four hours. The river has been very still.

8C.title: The First Trance
8C.description: At sunset the Professor draws the curtains in Dr Seward's study, lights a single lamp and puts his watch on a thread. Jonathan sits by the door. Quincey stands at the window with his rifle where you cannot see it. The Professor tells you to look at the flame and to listen to his voice. After a while you are not in the room. You are somewhere cold and wet with a low ceiling, and there are footsteps overhead and the sound of water against wood. The Professor's voice, far above you, asks what you see.

options.label: Tell him everything: the water, the creak of the timbers, the footsteps, the cold.
options.detail: He cannot help you if you leave things out, and he cannot get you out if he does not know where you are.

quote.speaker: Van Helsing
quote.text: Good. Good, Madam Mina. You are doing very well. Now, if you can, tell me what time it is.

options.outcome: The words come out of you without being chosen. Afterwards the Professor writes them down and reads them back, and you cannot remember saying a single one. "Water," he says. "A ship, and in a harbour, or at anchor. We shall find him."

options.label: Tell him about the water, but keep back the voice you thought you heard.
options.detail: It said your name. It said it kindly. You do not know whether it was real.

quote.speaker: Mina
quote.text: I thought I would hear a monster. I heard a man who sounded very much as though he were asking me to dinner.

options.outcome: You describe the cold and the wood and the water, and leave out the voice. When the Professor brings you out, he looks at you for longer than he needs to. He does not ask what you left out. You are not sure whether that is tact or fear.

options.label: Resist the trance at the last moment and wake yourself.
options.detail: You will not be a window for anyone, not even a friend. You will be a door, which opens from the inside.
